title: The Letters of Abelard and Heloise
text:
Peter Abelard was the most brilliant and famous teacher in Paris in the early twelfth century. Around 1116 he became tutor to Heloise, the young niece of a canon of Notre-Dame named Fulbert. Heloise was already known for her learning. Teacher and pupil fell in love. When she became pregnant, Abelard took her to his family in Brittany, where she gave birth to a son they called Astrolabe.

To appease her uncle, Abelard proposed marriage. Heloise argued against it, saying a marriage would harm his career and that she preferred love freely given. They married secretly anyway. Fulbert, believing Abelard meant to abandon her, sent men who attacked him at night and castrated him. Both then entered religious life, Heloise as a nun and later abbess of the Paraclete, a convent Abelard had founded.

Years later, around 1132, Abelard wrote a long account of his misfortunes. Heloise read it and wrote to him, beginning a series of letters that still survive. She told him, with stunning frankness, that she had entered the convent for him, not for God, that she would rather be called his mistress than an empress, and that she could not repent of her love. He answered as a monk and spiritual guide, urging her to turn her love to Christ.

Abelard died in 1142, and his body was brought to the Paraclete. When Heloise died two decades later, she was buried beside him.
lesson: Love that is written down honestly can survive loss and separation. Telling the truth about our feelings, even when it is unwelcome, is a form of fidelity.
location: Paris and the Paraclete, Champagne, France
source: Abelard, Historia Calamitatum; The Letters of Abelard and Heloise, trans. Betty Radice (1974)
caveat: A minority of scholars have questioned whether all the letters are authentic.
